chapter_title: Security Best Practices and Common Vulnerabilities

screens.title: Security Best Practices and Common Vulnerabilities
screens.subtitle: Why immutability means security safeguards must be deliberate and thorough

narration.text: Smart contracts are powerful but immutable. Once deployed, a contract’s code typically cannot be changed without careful migration, so security issues can cause irreversible loss of funds and reputational damage. In this lesson you will learn the mechanics behind the most frequent vulnerabilities — reentrancy and integer overflow/underflow — and the practical patterns and tools developers use to prevent them. You will see a concrete withdraw example that can be drained through a reentrancy exploit, and you will learn how the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and guard utilities prevent that behavior. You will also explore why older Solidity versions needed SafeMath for arithmetic safety and how access control mistakes or unbounded loops can create other exploit opportunities. By the end of this chapter you will be able to spot risky external calls, recognize where state updates must occur, and plan tests and static analysis to catch defects before deployment. Consider how a single external call in your code could let an attacker interrupt state updates — that perspective will guide every secure design choice you make.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Design smart contracts assuming external calls are malicious; update state first, then interact externally, and validate arithmetic and access control.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build and the reasoning behind them

narration.text: This first objectives slide explains what practical skills you will acquire and why they matter. You will learn to identify common smart contract vulnerabilities such as reentrancy and integer overflow. Identification means understanding the exact mechanics — for reentrancy, how an external call can reenter before state updates; for arithmetic issues, how wraparound silently corrupts balances. A second objective is to implement defensive code patterns: you will practice the Checks-Effects-Interactions order for stateful functions and learn when to use OpenZeppelin utilities like ReentrancyGuard. A third objective is to recognize access control failures and front-running risks, so you can apply correct visibility, modifiers, and commit-reveal techniques where appropriate. Finally, you will apply general security hygiene: minimizing external calls, avoiding unbounded loops, writing thorough tests, and running static analysis. Each objective is chosen to reduce real-world risk — these are the checks you run before deploying live value-bearing contracts. As you progress, focus on being able to explain why each mitigation prevents a specific exploit and how you would test for it.

narration.text: On this second objectives slide we focus on practice and assessment. You will refactor a vulnerable withdraw function to follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and, optionally, apply a ReentrancyGuard. This hands-on change tests your ability to place checks, update state, and then perform external interactions in the correct order. You will also convert arithmetic operations in older contracts to use SafeMath or equivalent wrappers to prevent wraparound errors. For access control, practice writing and testing modifiers such as onlyOwner or role checks, and include unit tests that assert unauthorized calls revert. Finally, you will run static analysis tools like Slither and MythX as part of your CI pipeline and interpret their findings. These exercises confirm not just that you can write safe code, but that you can explain why each change eliminates a specific risk. When preparing for assessment, ensure your tests cover attack scenarios and that you can explain the trade-offs of guard patterns versus architectural changes.

screens.title: Reentrancy vulnerability — how the withdraw example fails
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step walkthrough of the classic withdraw exploit

narration.text: Reentrancy happens when a contract performs an external call before it has finished updating its internal state, allowing a malicious counterparty to call back and run the same logic repeatedly. Consider a typical withdraw function that checks a balance, then sends Ether, and finally updates the stored balance. If the external transfer occurs before the state change, an attacker’s fallback can reenter the withdraw function and pass the same check repeatedly, draining funds. Concretely, the VulnerableBank contract deposits increase a balances mapping, and withdraw performs msg. sender. call with value before decreasing balances[msg. sender]. The attack sequence is: attacker deposits, calls withdraw, the contract sends Ether which triggers the attacker’s fallback, the fallback calls withdraw again while the original balance is unchanged, and this repeats until the contract’s funds are exhausted. A common misconception is thinking that only high-level logic or complex calls produce reentrancy; in fact a single simple external call that forwards gas can be enough. The key takeaway is to treat every external call as a potential entry point for recursion and design state updates to make repeated calls ineffective. Reflect: where in your functions might an external call allow a second entry?

keyIdea.title: Reentrancy defined
keyIdea.text: An external call can enable repeated callbacks into a function before state changes complete, letting an attacker exploit unchanged state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Reentrancy Vulnerability
Vulnerable example
// VulnerableBank: withdraw shows external call before state change
function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
  require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

  // VULNERABILITY: External call before state update
  (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
  require(success, "Transfer failed");

  balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // State updated AFTER external call
}
Concrete example

An attacker contract receives the transfer and in its fallback calls withdraw again while balance is unchanged.

Sequence explained
  • Attacker deposits to set a positive balance.
  • Attacker calls withdraw, contract performs external call first.
  • Fallback executes and reenters withdraw; balance still unmodified.
  • Repeat until contract funds drained.
Common misconception

Developers sometimes assume simple transfers are safe; forwarding gas via call can still enable reentrancy. Never assume external addresses are benign.

Key Takeaway

Always update state before external calls; treat external calls as untrusted entry points.

screens.title: Checks → Effects → Interactions
screens.subtitle: A simple, enforceable order that prevents reentrancy exploits

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prescribes an order of operations that closes the reentrancy window. First, perform all condition checks: validate inputs, require that balances and allowances are sufficient, and guard against invalid parameters. Second, execute effects: update internal state variables so the contract’s representation reflects the intended change. Finally, perform interactions: make any external calls or transfers. The reason this order works is simple: if state changes are committed before an external call occurs, a reentrant call will see the already-updated state and fail any checks. For example, a withdraw should require balance >= amount, subtract the amount from balances[msg. sender], then call payable(msg. sender). call. Developers sometimes prefer using solidity’s transfer or send which forward only 2300 gas and constrain the callee, but call is often necessary for compatibility. For an extra guard, OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard provides a nonReentrant modifier that locks the function during execution. Note the trade-off: using transfer or send reduces reentrancy risk but can fail if the callee needs more gas; using call with Checks-Effects-Interactions keeps flexibility while defending state. How would you reorder a critical function in your code to follow this pattern?

keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: Checks first, then Effects, then Interactions — update state before making external calls to stop reentrant withdrawals.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Checks-Effects-Interactions
Pattern
1. CHECKS

Validate inputs and state conditions using require statements. Example: require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount).

2. EFFECTS

Update internal state immediately. Example: balances[msg.sender] -= amount.

3. INTERACTIONS

Make external calls only after state is safe. Example: (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: amount}("");

Key Takeaway

Apply this order in every state-changing function that performs external calls.

Secure withdraw example
// Secure pattern in withdraw
require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");
balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // EFFECTS
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: _amount}(""); // INTERACTIONS
require(success, "Transfer failed");
When to add ReentrancyGuard

As an extra layer, nonReentrant prevents reentry by locking the function during execution; combine it with the pattern for defense in depth.

screens.title: Attacker contract and call-stack mechanics
screens.subtitle: How an attacking fallback reenters and drains funds

narration.text: Understanding the attacker’s contract clarifies why reentrancy succeeds. An attacker deposits a small amount and then calls withdraw. The vulnerable contract performs an external call that sends Ether to msg. sender, invoking the attacker’s fallback. In that fallback, the attacker checks whether the bank still has funds and calls withdraw again. Because the original contract has not yet reduced the attacker’s stored balance, the require check still passes, allowing another transfer. This sequence repeats until the bank is empty. A concrete code example provided in the chapter shows an Attacker contract with a fallback that conditionally calls withdraw while the target has sufficient balance. Many developers misunderstand gas mechanics: using transfer or send restricts forwarded gas to 2300, which often prevents reentrancy because the fallback cannot perform an external call again. However, transfer may fail with some recipients, and call is sometimes required. The right defense is to update state before any external call, and to use guard modifiers when appropriate. When you audit a contract, always inspect the call sites and think like the fallback — what could it call back into, and with what state?

keyIdea.title: Attack flow
keyIdea.text: An attacker’s fallback can call back into the vulnerable function if state was not updated, repeating the withdraw sequence until funds are drained.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Attacker Contract Mechanics
Attacker example
contract Attacker {
  VulnerableBank public vulnerableBank;
  uint256 public attackAmount = 1 ether;

  constructor(address _vulnerableBankAddress) {
    vulnerableBank = VulnerableBank(_vulnerableBankAddress);
  }

  function attack() public payable {
    vulnerableBank.deposit{value: attackAmount}();
    vulnerableBank.withdraw(attackAmount);
  }

  fallback() external payable {
    if (address(vulnerableBank).balance >= attackAmount) {
      vulnerableBank.withdraw(attackAmount); // Reenter
    }
  }
}
Call stack explanation
  • The bank calls msg.sender, which triggers the attacker fallback.
  • The fallback calls back into the bank, creating nested calls on the stack.
  • Because state wasn’t changed, the bank’s checks still succeed each time.
Gas and transfer nuances

transfer/send forward 2300 gas which often prevents fallback from calling out. But they can fail with certain recipients; call forwards flexible gas and must be used with care and proper patterns.

Pro tip

When auditing, explicitly mark every external call and check whether state has already been mutated to render reentry harmless.

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.subtitle: Why arithmetic bounds matter and how SafeMath helped older contracts

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow occur when arithmetic exceeds a type’s maximum or minimum, causing wraparound in older Solidity versions. For example, a uint256 at its maximum plus one wrapped to zero in Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0. That silent wrap can corrupt balances or permit unauthorized state transitions. The practical consequence is immediate: if a balance wraps to zero, checks relying on it will behave incorrectly and may grant unintended privileges or allow drained funds. Solidity 0.8.0 and later revert when overflow or underflow occurs, mitigating this class of bug. For older contracts, developers used OpenZeppelin’s SafeMath library. SafeMath provides functions like add and sub that perform checks and revert on overflow or underflow. A concrete example: if you write balance = balance + amount in older code, replace it with balance = balance. add(amount) after using SafeMath. A common misconception is that compiler upgrades eliminate all arithmetic risks; legacy contracts and libraries still in use require careful review. Key takeaway: verify compiler version and either rely on built-in checked arithmetic or apply SafeMath consistently and test boundary conditions. Integer Overflow and Underflow means use compiler checks or safemath to ensure arithmetic does not wrap and silently corrupt contract state.. In practical terms, why arithmetic bounds matter and how safemath helped older contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Arithmetic safety
keyIdea.text: Use compiler checks or SafeMath to ensure arithmetic does not wrap and silently corrupt contract state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Integer Overflow / Underflow
Problem

If arithmetic wraps, balances or counters can jump to unexpected values. This can cause logic that checks those values to behave incorrectly.

// Example behavior before Solidity 0.8.0:
uint256 x = 2**256 - 1;
x++; // x becomes 0 (wraparound)

uint256 y = 0;
y--; // y becomes 2**256 - 1
Defenses
Compiler checks (Solidity ≥ 0.8.0)

Arithmetic now reverts on overflow/underflow, removing many silent wrap issues.

SafeMath (older compilers)

Use SafeMath.add/sub to perform bounds-checked arithmetic and revert on error.

Common misconception

Assuming compiler upgrades protect legacy code. Old contracts and libraries still in production must be audited and updated where possible.

screens.title: Access Control and Visibility
screens.subtitle: Protecting sensitive functions with modifiers and correct visibility

narration.text: Access control mistakes let unauthorized users trigger sensitive behavior. In Solidity, function visibility and access modifiers are the first line of defense. For functions that manage funds, upgrade contracts, or change privileged state, require explicit guards such as onlyOwner or role checks. For example, an onlyOwner modifier checks msg. sender equals owner and reverts otherwise. Always prefer explicit modifiers or role-based access to implicit assumptions. A common mistake is leaving a function public or omitting a require guard because the developer believes the call path prevents misuse; on-chain attackers operate outside assumed call flows. Another error is relying on tx. origin for authorization; using msg. sender and proper modifiers is safer. When designing an access model, document roles and test each negative case: attempts by unauthorized accounts should revert with a clear error. Consider using established libraries that implement role hierarchies and standards; they reduce the chance of subtle mistakes. Ask yourself: who should never be able to call this function, and how will tests prove that? Access Control and Visibility means use explicit modifiers and role checks for sensitive functions; document roles and include tests for unauthorized callers.. In practical terms, protecting sensitive functions with modifiers and correct visibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access control
keyIdea.text: Use explicit modifiers and role checks for sensitive functions; document roles and include tests for unauthorized callers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Access Control & Visibility
Pattern
modifier onlyOwner() {
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this");
  _;
}

function sensitiveAction() public onlyOwner {
  // privileged logic
}
Concrete example

Protect all administrators and upgrade functions with role checks and include tests that call them from unauthorized addresses.

Common mistakes
  • Leaving functions public without guards because they appear unreachable.
  • Using tx.origin for authorization instead of msg.sender.
  • Failing to test negative cases for unauthorized callers.
Pro Tip

Adopt role-based libraries from trusted sources and write unit tests that attempt forbidden actions to ensure they revert cleanly.

screens.title: Front-running and mitigation strategies
screens.subtitle: Why pending transactions are observable and what to do about it

narration.text: Front-running occurs when an observer sees a pending transaction in the mempool and submits their own transaction with a higher gas price to be mined earlier, changing the outcome to their advantage. This can happen in trading contracts, auctions, or any protocol where pending transactions reveal useful information. A simple mitigation is a commit-reveal scheme: users first submit a commitment that hides the secret (for example a hash of a bid), then later reveal the secret in a second transaction. This prevents observers from acting on revealed data because the important value only becomes public after the reveal step. Another mitigation is using relayers or private transaction submission so that sensitive transactions are not visible in public mempools. A common misconception is that higher gas price alone protects your transaction; it only affects ordering, not confidentiality. Commit-reveal introduces UX friction and requires careful timing; relayers add trust or infrastructure complexity. The practical question is whether your application can tolerate a two-step flow or needs architectural changes to avoid exposing sensitive data in the mempool. Front-running and mitigation strategies means mempool visibility allows adversaries to reorder transactions; commit-reveal or private submission reduces exposed information.. In practical terms, why pending transactions are observable and what to do about it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Front-running insight
keyIdea.text: Mempool visibility allows adversaries to reorder transactions; commit-reveal or private submission reduces exposed information.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Front-running
Problem

An attacker observes a pending transaction and submits a competing transaction with higher gas to be included earlier, altering outcomes.

Example: DEX trade

A trade that will move price can be front-run by submitting a buy first and a sell after to capture value.

Mitigations
Commit-Reveal

Two-step process hides details until reveal, preventing profitable reordering based on content.

Private submission / relayers

Avoid exposing sensitive txs to public mempool, but weigh trust and infrastructure costs.

Key takeaway

Design for confidentiality of sensitive inputs or accept UX trade-offs for commit-reveal flows.

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS) and gas limits
screens.subtitle: How unbounded loops or user-controlled data can make functions unusable

narration.text: Denial of Service in smart contracts often arises from functions that scale with user-controlled data, like iterating over an ever-growing array of addresses. An attacker can fill that array or add entries that make the loop expensive enough to exceed the gas limit, preventing anyone from successfully calling the function. Another DoS vector is locking funds through conditional logic that fails and reverts when a specific address behaves unexpectedly. The practical defenses are to avoid unbounded on-chain iteration, prefer pull over push payment models, and shard or paginate state so operations remain bounded. For example, rather than iterating through all participants in one transaction, provide per-user claim functions or batched processing with explicit limits. Developers sometimes think simply adding more gas will help; miner and network limits still exist and user transactions must fit those constraints. Testing should include stress scenarios where data grows and simulate attackers trying to push costs above allowable ranges. The key question to ask when designing functions is: can a user or attacker make this operation unaffordable or impossible for others? Denial of Service (DoS) and gas limits means avoid unbounded loops and user-controlled growth; use bounded operations, pull payments, and batching to keep functions callable.. In practical terms, how unbounded loops or user-controlled data can make functions unusable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DoS insight
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded loops and user-controlled growth; use bounded operations, pull payments, and batching to keep functions callable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Denial of Service & Gas
Problem patterns
  • Unbounded loops over user-controlled arrays.
  • Push payment models that iterate over many recipients in one tx.
  • Conditional logic that can be forced to revert for all users.
Concrete mitigation

Switch to pull payments where each user claims their funds, and implement batching with explicit limits to bound gas per call.

Testing tips
  • Simulate large arrays and stress-test gas usage.
  • Write negative tests where an attacker grows state to try to break operations.
Key Takeaway

Design every function to remain bounded and test growth scenarios to prevent DoS through gas exhaustion.

screens.title: Security Best Practices, Testing and Tools
screens.subtitle: A checklist: calls, gas, state, fallback, testing, audits, and static analysis

narration.text: This final lesson on defenses consolidates practical best practices and tooling. Treat every external call as potentially malicious: minimize them, isolate them, and always apply Checks-Effects-Interactions when calls are necessary. Be mindful of gas; avoid expensive on-chain computation and unbounded loops. Initialize and document state variables explicitly so their defaults do not surprise you. Keep fallback functions minimal and non-payable unless needed; they should log or revert rather than perform complex state changes. Testing is essential: write unit tests, integration tests, and fuzz tests that simulate edge conditions and attack sequences. Use test frameworks to assert reverts and to simulate gas constraints. Use static analysis tools such as Slither and MythX to find class-level issues automatically; interpret alerts and prioritize fixes based on exploitability. For production, obtain professional audits and consider upgradability patterns only when you accept their security trade-offs. Finally, document your defenses so auditors and future maintainers understand the rationale. Ask yourself as a checklist: have I minimized external calls, bounded loops, secured arithmetic, protected access, and written tests that simulate adversaries? Security Best Practices, Testing and Tools means minimize external calls, bound loops, secure arithmetic and access, write exhaustive tests, and run static analysis and audits.. In practical terms, a checklist: calls, gas, state, fallback, testing, audits, and static analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concept cards to anchor core ideas

narration.text: Summarizing the essentials helps cement secure habits. First, reentrancy: always assume external calls might reenter your contract. Updating state before making external calls and optionally using ReentrancyGuard are practical defenses. Second, integer safety: know your compiler’s behavior. Solidity 0.8 and later revert on overflow and underflow, but older contracts need SafeMath to prevent silent wraparound. Third, access control and gas considerations: protect privileged functions with explicit modifiers and avoid unbounded loops or push models that enable denial-of-service. These three ideas — restrict external interactions, make arithmetic explicit and tested, and keep operations bounded with clear access control — form the backbone of safe smart contract design. As you return to code, keep these check points at hand and add tests and static analysis to confirm your defenses. Which one will you verify first in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Defend by design: update state first, check arithmetic boundaries, and control access and gas usage.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you code or deploy

narration.text: A short checklist to carry forward: one, follow Checks-Effects-Interactions and consider ReentrancyGuard to stop callback-based drains. Two, confirm arithmetic safety by relying on Solidity 0.8’s checked math or applying SafeMath in older contracts, and always test edge values. Three, enforce explicit access control and design functions to be bounded and testable to reduce DoS and front-running risk. These reminders are intentionally concise because they are the questions you should ask every time you change code or review pull requests. Before deployment, run your full test suite, scan with static analysis tools like Slither and MythX, and document your choices for auditors. If you adopt these practices consistently, you will dramatically reduce the most common, high-impact vulnerabilities. What to Remember means order operations, verify arithmetic, and protect access — test and analyze before you deploy.. In practical terms, three compact reminders before you code or deploy. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
